In this episode of Backstage with Millionaires, we take a deep dive into the rise, fall, and uncertain future of boAt—one of India’s most recognizable consumer electronics brands. From becoming the world’s fifth-largest wearable brand in 2020 to facing declining revenues and leadership changes, boAt’s journey is a classic case of rapid growth followed by equally sharp challenges.

The story begins during the COVID-19 pandemic, when boAt experienced explosive growth. With increased screen time and work-from-home culture, demand for affordable audio products surged. BoAt, already a well-established brand in India, capitalized on this trend and became a household name. Simultaneously, the company entered the smartwatch segment in late 2020, riding the wave of health-conscious consumers. This new category alone generated nearly ₹900 crore in revenue within two years, contributing significantly to the company’s total revenue, which peaked at over ₹3,300 crore in FY23.

However, as the pandemic-driven demand subsided, cracks began to appear. The smartwatch segment, once a major growth driver, saw a steep decline. Consumers became more discerning and began favoring higher-quality, premium devices over budget options. Entry-level smartwatches—boAt’s core offering—failed to meet rising expectations in terms of accuracy and performance. As a result, the overall smartwatch market in India shrank significantly, and boAt’s revenue from this segment dropped by over 60% in just one year.

At the same time, boAt’s core audio business also started losing momentum. The brand’s original edge—affordable products with trendy designs—was no longer unique. Increased competition from both Indian and global brands led to commoditization of the category. In such markets, companies known primarily for affordability often struggle to maintain margins and differentiation.

Leadership instability added to the challenges. Co-founders Aman Gupta and Sameer Mehta stepped back from executive roles, and the company has seen multiple CEO changes in recent years. This kind of transition can be difficult, especially when the company is already navigating a declining market position.

Looking ahead, boAt is attempting a strategic shift toward the premium segment, focusing on higher-priced products and better technology. While this is a logical move, it comes with its own challenges. The premium audio and wearable space is dominated by established global players with strong brand equity and technological expertise. Repositioning boAt from a value-driven brand to a premium one will not be easy.

The company’s IPO journey has also faced hurdles. After postponing its initial public offering in 2022, boAt filed again in 2025 but may delay it once more. Concerns have also been raised about discrepancies in financial filings, which could impact investor confidence.

Beyond boAt, the episode also covers major developments in the Indian startup ecosystem. Urban Company’s InstaHelp has crossed 1 million monthly bookings within a year of launch, emerging as a fast-scaling but currently loss-making business. Meanwhile, companies like Zetwerk and Rentomojo are preparing for IPOs, and several startups—including Bachatt, Amaha, BeastLife, Sign3, and Epik—have raised fresh funding.

Overall, this episode explores how quickly fortunes can change in the startup world and raises an important question: can boAt successfully reinvent itself, or will it follow the path of once-dominant brands that failed to adapt?

snippet.description:

Once India’s No.2 e-commerce giant, Snapdeal was seen as the next Flipkart. Within a few years, it collapsed from a $6.5 billion valuation to near disappearance. This video tells the full untold story of Snapdeal — how it rose, how it fell, and the brutal lessons every startup founder must learn to avoid the same fate.

----------------

00:00 Intro
00:50 Rise of Snapdeal

Around 2010, Snapdeal was one of India’s most promising startups, second only to Flipkart in market share and valuation. Founded by Kunal Bahl and Rohit Bansal, Snapdeal began as a deals and discount coupon platform called MoneySaver. They printed and sold coupon booklets and later shifted online as Snapdeal.com, connecting buyers with shops through online deals.

Snapdeal grew rapidly, attracted massive funding from global investors like eBay, BlackRock, and SoftBank, and reached a $6.5 billion valuation. The founders were inspired by Alibaba’s model and decided to convert Snapdeal into a full-fledged e-commerce marketplace. Their aggressive expansion, acquisitions, and marketing campaigns made them a household name.

However, the same aggression became their downfall. Snapdeal started chasing vanity metrics like GMV (Gross Merchandise Value) instead of focusing on customer satisfaction and experience. Poor product quality, fake sellers, and unreliable delivery led to massive customer dissatisfaction. Sellers also complained about high commissions and lack of support.

The company poured hundreds of millions into advertising, discounts, and unnecessary acquisitions like Freecharge, without strengthening its core business. Revenues rose but losses exploded — crossing ₹4,600 crores in FY 2017. Even investors like SoftBank lost confidence and wrote off huge amounts. Snapdeal’s valuation fell from $6.5 billion to $1 billion. A proposed merger with Flipkart failed, and the founders had to lay off employees, sell Freecharge for a fraction of its purchase price, and launch “Snapdeal 2.0” — a low-cost marketplace for value-conscious buyers.

Today, Snapdeal continues to operate, but far from its past glory. It stands as one of India’s most dramatic startup case studies — a story of ambition, speed, and strategic mistakes.

From this journey, we can draw 4 powerful startup lessons:

1. Focus on customer experience first, growth later.

This is the tragic tale of a once great, this is the rise and downfall of SAAB.



Saab’s history begins in 1937 in the small Swedish city of Linkoping, located 120 miles south east of Stockholm. The company originally produced aircrafts, especially fighter aircrafts for the Swedish Air Force, which were planned to be used by Sweden to defend its neutrality in World War II. After the war ended, demand for military aircrafts dropped and the company decided to diversify its business and so the Saab Automobile division was created. Work on the first Saab automobile was started in 1945, under the X9248 codename. Soon, the project became known as Project 92 (Saab’s previous product was the Saab 91, a single engine aircraft). With the automobile project advancing, the company decided that car production will take place in one of their facilities in Trolhattan, a city on Sweden’s North Sea coast, about 200 miles away from Stockholm. In 1948, work started on converting the existing facility to allow automobile assembly and soon the Saab Automobiles’ headquartered was also moved to Trolhattan, where it remained ever since.

snippet.title: Yahoo’s Downfall Story to Google
snippet.description:
Yahoo was once the king of the internet. In the late 1990s and early 2000s, if you wanted to find anything online, you went to Yahoo. They had search, email, news, and nearly everything else you could imagine. At their peak in 2000, they were worth $125 billion dollars—one of the most valuable companies on the planet.
But then they started saying no to everything.
In 1998, two Stanford graduate students named Larry Page and Sergey Brin came to Yahoo with a new search engine called Google. They offered to sell it for just $1 million. Yahoo passed. They didn't think search technology mattered that much.
Four years later, Google was growing fast. Yahoo realized their mistake and tried to buy Google for $3 billion in 2002. But by then, Google wanted $5 billion. Yahoo thought that was too expensive and walked away again.
Then in 2006, a young Mark Zuckerberg was willing to sell Facebook. Yahoo offered $1 billion, and Zuckerberg agreed. But when Yahoo's stock dipped slightly, they lowered their offer to $850 million. Zuckerberg was insulted and killed the deal.
The worst decision came in 2008. Microsoft offered to buy Yahoo for $44.6 billion in cash—one of the largest acquisition offers in tech history. Yahoo's co-founder and CEO, Jerry Yang, rejected it. He thought it was too low. Shareholders were furious. Microsoft walked away and never came back.
After that, Yahoo went into a slow decline. They cycled through multiple CEOs. They lost users to Google and Facebook. In 2013, they discovered they'd been hacked—3 billion user accounts were compromised in the largest data breach ever recorded.
By 2017, Verizon bought Yahoo for just $4.5 billion. A company once worth $125 billion, that turned down $44.6 billion in cash, sold for less than 5 billion.
Today, Yahoo still exists. The email still works. But it's a ghost of what it once was—a reminder that in tech, saying no to the wrong things can cost you everything.
